## Generate-and-Select: The First Wave {#sec-first-wave}

| # | Source | Summary |
|---|---|---|

| 2 | [OPRO (ICLR 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409) | Meta-prompt, trajectory, ascending sort |
| 3 | [InstructZero (ICML 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03082) | Bayesian optimization in soft-prompt space |

### From Manual Search to Automated Proposals

The first generation of prompt optimization algorithms (2022--2023) shared a simple but powerful idea: let the LLM itself propose candidate prompts, then use a scoring function to select the best ones. The progression from APE to OPRO to InstructZero traces a path from one-shot proposal to iterative refinement to surrogate-guided search.

To ground this concretely, imagine applying each algorithm to our support ticket triage system. APE would generate 50 candidate instructions for classifying urgency and pick the one with the highest accuracy. OPRO would start with those candidates, but then iteratively refine them, using a meta-prompt that remembers which triage instructions scored well and which scored poorly. InstructZero would search a continuous proxy space to find instructions without ever directly searching over discrete text.

### APE: Prompts as Programs to Be Synthesized

APE ([Zhou et al., ICLR 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01910), November 2022) established the foundational framing: treat the task model's instruction as a program to be synthesized by another LLM. The core optimization objective:

$$
\rho^* = \arg\max_\rho \; f(\rho) = \arg\max_\rho \; \mathbb{E}_{(Q, A)} \left[ f(\rho, Q, A) \right]
$$ {#eq-ape}

where $\rho$ is the instruction, $Q$ is the input query, $A$ is the expected answer, and $f$ is a per-sample score.

APE generates candidate instructions in two modes:

- **Forward mode**: Present the LLM with input-output demonstrations and ask it to infer the instruction. The model sees examples of $\{(Q_1, A_1), (Q_2, A_2), \ldots\}$ and generates instructions that could have produced these mappings. This samples approximately from $P(\rho \mid \mathcal{D}, f(\rho) \text{ is high})$.

- **Reverse mode**: Use an infilling model (T5, GLM) to fill in a blank instruction positioned within a template. The instruction can be placed anywhere in the prompt, not just at the end.

For scoring, APE offers two functions. **Execution accuracy** is the hard metric: $f(\rho, Q, A) = \mathbb{1}[M([\rho; Q]) = A]$. **Log probability** provides a softer signal: $f(\rho, Q, A) = \log P(A \mid [\rho; Q])$, which gives fine-grained guidance even when the model's top prediction is wrong.

The clever part is **adaptive filtering**: evaluate all candidates cheaply on a small subset, keep the top performers, evaluate survivors on a new subset, repeat. This is tournament selection. Low-quality prompts are eliminated early, saving the expensive full evaluation for the handful of finalists. APE matched or exceeded human-written prompts on 24 of 24 Instruction Induction tasks, and the best APE-generated prompt sometimes surpassed the best human prompt.

For our triage system, APE would take 10--20 examples of (customer message, correct urgency) pairs, ask the LLM to infer what instruction could have produced these classifications, generate 50 candidates, score them, and return the winner. Simple, effective, and entirely one-shot. The limitation: no learning from failures. If the best prompt scores 78%, APE has no mechanism to ask "why did it fail on the other 22%?" and iterate.

### Self-Refine: The Simplest Feedback Loop

Before OPRO introduced iterative *prompt* refinement, Self-Refine ([Madaan et al., NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651)) showed that LLMs can iteratively improve their own *outputs*. The loop is straightforward:

$$
y_0 = M(p, x), \quad e_0 = M(\text{"Critique"}, y_0), \quad y_1 = M(p, x, y_0, e_0)
$$

Generate an output, critique it, revise it. The critique is the key innovation: the LLM generates natural language feedback about what is wrong with its own answer, then uses that feedback to produce a better answer.

The distinction matters: Self-Refine improves the *output* while keeping the prompt fixed. The prompt itself never changes. This pattern is output-level optimization, not parameter-level optimization. If our triage prompt consistently misclassifies billing complaints, Self-Refine would fix each individual misclassification at inference time, but it would not fix the prompt to prevent future misclassifications. That boundary is important. Every method in the rest of this chapter operates at the prompt level: they change the instruction itself, not just the outputs it produces.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: Self-Refine and TextGrad do the same thing"}
Both use LLM-generated feedback to improve something. But Self-Refine improves the *output* (the answer to a specific question) while keeping the prompt fixed. TextGrad (@sec-textual-gradients) improves the *prompt* (or any variable in a computation graph) by propagating feedback backward. The optimization target is different: output-level vs. parameter-level. Self-Refine is test-time refinement; TextGrad is compile-time optimization.
:::

::: {.exercise-mcq correct="D"}

A team deploys a triage system using Self-Refine. Each ticket's classification is generated, critiqued, and revised by the LLM before being shown to agents. Accuracy on a held-out set looks strong (88%), but a month later, the same systematic failure pattern (billing complaints misclassified as low urgency) keeps recurring. A colleague suggests switching to OPRO. What specific advantage would OPRO provide over Self-Refine for this problem?

- OPRO uses a more capable LLM that would not make billing-related mistakes
- OPRO evaluates on more examples per iteration, so it would catch the billing pattern statistically
- OPRO generates natural language critiques that explain *why* the prompt fails on billing cases
- OPRO would rewrite the *prompt itself* to include billing-specific guidance, preventing the failure from recurring on every new input

::: {.feedback-correct}
Correct! Self-Refine operates at the *output level*: it critiques and revises each individual answer while keeping the prompt fixed. The prompt never learns to handle billing complaints, so the same failure recurs on every new billing ticket. OPRO operates at the *prompt level*: it would iteratively rewrite the triage instruction itself, potentially adding guidance about billing complaints, prior escalations, and financial impact. The root cause (the prompt) gets fixed, not just its symptoms. (Note: natural language critiques are TextGrad's approach, not OPRO's; OPRO uses scalar scores.)
:::

::: {.feedback-incorrect}
The key distinction is *what gets optimized*. Self-Refine improves individual outputs but keeps the prompt fixed. OPRO rewrites the prompt itself through iterative optimization. The advantage is not about model capability, evaluation size, or natural language critiques (that is TextGrad's approach). OPRO would modify the triage instruction to include billing-specific guidance, preventing the same failure pattern from recurring on every new input. This is the difference between output-level and parameter-level optimization.
:::

:::

### OPRO: The LLM as Its Own Optimizer

OPRO ([Yang et al., ICLR 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409), September 2023) introduced the idea that became the foundation for most subsequent work: use an LLM not just to propose prompts, but to iteratively optimize them by learning from a history of past attempts. The mathematical formulation is the same as @eq-apo-objective:

$$
p^* = \arg\max_p \; S(p) = \arg\max_p \; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}\{M_\theta(p, x_i) = y_i\}
$$

The innovation is in the optimization loop. OPRO constructs a **meta-prompt** with three components:

1. **Meta-instructions** (how to optimize): Text telling the optimizer LLM what to do. Example: "Generate a new instruction that achieves a higher accuracy than all previous instructions."

2. **Optimization trajectory** (what has been tried): A list of past prompts and their scores, sorted in ascending order from worst to best. Example: `("Classify the sentiment": 62.3%)`, `("Determine if positive or negative": 71.5%)`, `("Analyze the emotional tone carefully": 78.1%)`.

3. **Task exemplars** (what the task looks like): 3 randomly sampled input-output examples from the training set, showing the format and expected behavior.

The algorithm repeats: generate 8 candidates from the meta-prompt at temperature 1.0 for diversity, evaluate each on the training set at temperature 0 for determinism, add the new (prompt, score) pairs to the trajectory, and keep only the top 20 entries. After up to 200 steps, return the highest-scoring prompt.

The ascending sort is surprisingly important. OPRO found that sorting from worst-to-best significantly outperforms descending or random ordering. The hypothesis: LLMs exhibit a **recency bias** where tokens closer to the end of the context window have more influence on generation. By placing the best prompts last, the optimizer is more likely to generate variations of high-scoring candidates.

For our triage system, OPRO's meta-prompt might look like:

> *"You are an optimizer. Below are previous triage instructions and their accuracy scores. Generate a new instruction that achieves higher accuracy."*
>
> *("Classify urgency": 72.0%)*
>
> *("Evaluate ticket urgency based on customer tone": 78.3%)*
>
> *("Carefully assess financial impact, emotional distress, and time sensitivity. Classify as low, medium, or high urgency": 84.1%)*
>
> *[3 example tickets with correct urgency labels]*

The optimizer LLM reads this trajectory, notices the upward trend, and generates a candidate that tries to push the accuracy higher. It learns, through in-context learning, what kinds of instructions work for this task.

OPRO's most celebrated finding: on GSM8K with PaLM 2-L, it discovered "Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step" (80.2% accuracy, up from the 71.8% baseline of "Let's think step by step"). On BBH, OPRO outperformed the baseline by over 5% on 19 of 23 tasks.

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: Why ascending order? What does this reveal about LLM optimization?"}
OPRO's ascending sort exploits the recency bias of autoregressive LLMs: tokens near the end of the prompt have outsized influence on generation. By placing the best solutions last, OPRO steers the optimizer toward generating variations of high-scoring candidates. This is a form of implicit exploitation. But it raises a deeper question: if the optimization algorithm's effectiveness depends on such LLM-specific quirks (recency bias, sensitivity to example ordering), how robust are these methods? GPO later showed that *relevance-based* trajectory retrieval (selecting semantically similar past prompts, regardless of position) outperforms recency by +15%. The ordering trick works, but it is not the deepest solution. The field is gradually shifting from exploiting LLM biases to providing LLMs with genuinely informative optimization context.
:::

::: {.exercise-order correct="D,B,A,C"}

OPRO's optimization loop has four steps that repeat each iteration. Arrange them in correct order:

- Evaluate each candidate on the training set at temperature 0 for determinism
- Generate 8 candidate prompts from the meta-prompt at temperature 1.0 for diversity
- Return the highest-scoring prompt after convergence or 200 steps
- Construct the meta-prompt with meta-instructions, ascending-sorted trajectory, and task exemplars

::: {.order-feedback}
**Correct order: D, B, A, C.** First, OPRO constructs the meta-prompt (D) by assembling the meta-instructions, the trajectory of past (prompt, score) pairs sorted worst-to-best, and randomly sampled task exemplars. Then it generates 8 diverse candidates (B) at high temperature. Each candidate is evaluated deterministically (A) at temperature 0. After adding the new (prompt, score) pairs to the trajectory and checking the stopping condition, the best prompt is returned (C). The ascending sort in step D is critical: it places the best prompts last, exploiting recency bias to steer the optimizer toward high-scoring variations.
:::

:::

### SPO: Dropping the Ground-Truth Requirement

A significant limitation of APE and OPRO is that they require labeled ground truth for scoring: you need $(x, y)$ pairs where $y$ is the correct answer. For many real-world tasks (creative writing, customer service quality, summarization), no single correct answer exists. How do you score a triage prompt when "good" is a judgment call?

SPO ([Xiang et al., EMNLP 2025 Findings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06855)) solves this with a simple but powerful insight: instead of comparing outputs to ground-truth answers (*Output vs. Ground Truth*, or OvG), compare outputs from two different prompts against each other (*Output vs. Output*, or OvO). An LLM judge receives two sets of outputs (from the current best prompt and a new candidate) and picks the better set. The algorithm is hill-climbing: if the new prompt's outputs win, it becomes the new best; otherwise, the old prompt survives.

The mechanism has two components. First, an *optimizer LLM* generates a new candidate prompt by reading the current prompt and its outputs, then analyzing what could be improved. The optimizer never sees ground-truth labels or scores; it works entirely from the outputs themselves. Second, an *evaluator LLM* performs pairwise comparison of the two prompts' outputs, picking the set that better meets the task requirements. Four rounds of randomized evaluation mitigate position bias.

The efficiency is striking. SPO uses just 3 sample questions (without answers) per iteration, and 8 LLM calls total per iteration. Across five benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, AGIEval-MATH Level 5, LIAR, WSC, BBH-Navigate), SPO achieved 66.9% average accuracy at $0.15 per dataset, compared to OPRO's 66.6% at $4.51 and TextGrad's 63.9% at $13.14. SPO achieves comparable or better performance at 1.1% to 5.6% of existing methods' costs. The practical implication: prompt optimization no longer requires a labeled evaluation set, which opens the door to optimizing prompts for any task where an LLM can judge output quality.

### BPO: Learning a Prompt-Rewriting Function

Every method discussed so far searches for prompts at the *task level*: one prompt per task, optimized through iteration. BPO ([Cheng et al., ACL 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04155)) takes a categorically different approach. Instead of searching for a single task-level prompt, BPO trains a dedicated seq2seq model that rewrites individual user prompts to elicit better responses from any target LLM.

The method has three stages. First, BPO collects preference data from four public datasets (OASST1, HH-RLHF, Chatbot Arena, Alpaca-GPT4), each containing triples of (user prompt, preferred response, dispreferred response). Second, ChatGPT analyzes each triple to identify what makes the preferred response better, then rewrites the original prompt to explicitly encourage those qualities. For example, the user prompt "Write a story ending with 'Are they really happy?'" becomes "Write a story that naturally builds toward the question. Ensure the story ends with the question without providing a response." This step produces approximately 14,000 (original, rewritten) prompt pairs. Third, a LLaMA-2-7B-chat model is fine-tuned on these pairs as a standard seq2seq rewriter.

At inference time, BPO is a single forward pass: the user's prompt enters the rewriter, and the rewritten version is sent to whatever target LLM is in use. No search, no iteration, no scoring. The rewriter is model-agnostic because it learns general patterns of human preference (explanation generation, hint provision, safety enhancement) rather than model-specific tricks. BPO-aligned ChatGPT yields a 22% win-rate increase over the original, and the same rewriter improves GPT-4 by 10%. Remarkably, BPO outperforms both PPO and DPO as an alignment method while being additive with them: combining DPO training with BPO yields 30% win-rate gains on Vicuna models.

The conceptual distinction from APE and OPRO is important. APE and OPRO optimize a *single prompt template per task* through search. BPO trains a *rewriting model* that transforms *any individual prompt* into a better version, amortizing the optimization cost into a one-time training step. This is amortized optimization: the offline training replaces the per-task search entirely. The trade-off is that BPO requires a training phase with preference data, while APE and OPRO work from a handful of examples.

This scoring function connects to a broader point: the scoring function $F$ in @eq-apo-objective can itself be a **learned reward model** $R_\varphi$ trained on human preferences. Instead of accuracy, we optimize:

$$
p^* = \arg\max_p \; \mathbb{E}_{y \sim M_T(x; p)} \left[ R_\varphi(p, x, y) \right]
$$

SPO and BPO represent two poles of how preference signals can replace ground truth. SPO uses pairwise comparison at test time (cheap, no training data needed). BPO uses preference data at training time (expensive to train, free at inference). Both eliminate the dependence on labeled $(x, y)$ pairs that constrains APE and OPRO to tasks with known correct answers.

### InstructZero: Bayesian Optimization in Disguise

InstructZero ([Chen et al., ICML 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03082), June 2023) introduced an elegant indirection. Instead of searching directly in the intractable space of discrete instructions, it optimizes a continuous soft prompt $z$ on an open-source LLM, which then generates a discrete instruction $I(z)$ for the black-box target LLM.

The soft prompt $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a continuous vector that can be optimized with Bayesian optimization (BO) (see @sec-math-bo for a review of BO, GP surrogates, and acquisition functions). At each step, BO selects a promising $z$ based on an acquisition function (Expected Improvement), the open-source LLM converts $z$ into a natural language instruction $I(z)$, and the instruction is evaluated on the black-box LLM. An instruction-coupled kernel captures the relationship between soft prompts and the instructions they produce.

The result: InstructZero achieved the best performance on all 32 BIG-Bench Instruction Induction tasks compared to APE and other baselines. The key insight is that BO is extremely sample-efficient (it builds a probabilistic model of the objective function), which makes it well-suited to the expensive-evaluation setting of prompt optimization.

::: {.exercise-mcq correct="B"}

InstructZero optimizes a continuous soft prompt $z$ on an open-source LLM, which then generates a discrete instruction for the target LLM. A colleague suggests: "Why not skip the indirection and apply Bayesian optimization directly to the discrete instruction strings?" What is the fundamental obstacle?

- Discrete instructions are too long for the acquisition function to evaluate
- Bayesian optimization requires a continuous input space to fit its Gaussian process surrogate; discrete text has no natural metric space for the GP to interpolate over
- The target LLM cannot process instructions generated by Bayesian optimization
- Bayesian optimization only works when the objective function is convex, which prompt accuracy is not

::: {.feedback-correct}
Correct! A Gaussian process models the objective as a smooth function over a continuous input domain, using distances between points to interpolate. Discrete instruction text has no natural continuous metric space for the GP to operate in. InstructZero's soft prompt $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ provides exactly the continuous domain BO needs, and the open-source LLM bridges the continuous-to-discrete gap.
:::

::: {.feedback-incorrect}
The obstacle is not about instruction length, LLM compatibility, or convexity. Bayesian optimization fits a Gaussian process surrogate that interpolates between evaluated points using distances in input space. Discrete text strings have no natural continuous metric space for this interpolation. The soft prompt $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ provides the continuous domain the GP needs, and the open-source LLM translates vectors into natural language.
:::

:::

::: {.exercise-predict correct="A"}

You have just seen that all generate-and-select methods (APE, OPRO, InstructZero) receive only a scalar score as feedback. The next subsection will summarize the entire paradigm. Before reading it, predict: what is the *single most important limitation* that all these methods share, despite their differences in search strategy?

- They all know *how well* a prompt performed but not *why* it succeeded or failed, so they cannot target specific failure modes
- They all require ground-truth labels, making them inapplicable to open-ended tasks
- They all use the same optimizer model architecture, limiting the diversity of generated candidates

::: {.predict-reveal}
**The answer is A.** Despite their different search strategies (one-shot, trajectory-based, Bayesian surrogate), APE, OPRO, and InstructZero all receive only scalar feedback: a number. They know a prompt scored 78%, but not *which parts* of the prompt caused failures or *which direction* to change it. The text calls this the fundamental limitation that motivates the textual gradient methods of the next section, which provide directional feedback in natural language.
:::

:::

### The Progression

These first-wave methods form a clean progression in the richness of their optimization signal:

```{.d2}
direction: right
vars: {
  d2-config: {
    layout-engine: elk
  }
}

classes: {
  base: {
    style: {
      fill: "white"
      stroke: "#E5E7EB"
      stroke-width: 2
      shadow: true
      border-radius: 8
      font-size: 13
    }
  }
  input: {
    style: {
      stroke: "#6366F1"
      fill: "#EEF2FF"
      font-color: "#3730A3"
    }
  }
  process: {
    style: {
      stroke: "#10B981"
      fill: "#ECFDF5"
      font-color: "#065F46"
    }
  }
}

APE: "APE\nOne-shot proposal + filter\nNo iteration" {
  class: [base; input]
}
OPRO: "OPRO\nIterative refinement\nScalar trajectory memory" {
  class: [base; input]
}
IZ: "InstructZero\nBayesian surrogate\nContinuous proxy space" {
  class: [base; process]
}
SPO: "SPO / BPO\nNo ground truth needed\nPairwise comparison / learned rewriter" {
  class: [base; process]
}

APE -> OPRO: "adds iteration\n+ memory" {
  style.font-size: 11
}
OPRO -> IZ: "adds surrogate\nmodel" {
  style.font-size: 11
}
APE -> SPO: "drops ground\ntruth requirement" {
  style.font-size: 11
}
```

| Method | Search Strategy | Requires Labels? | Iterative? | Key Innovation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| APE | LLM proposal + tournament | Yes | No | Prompts as programs |
| Self-Refine | LLM critique + revision | No | Yes (outputs) | LLM self-feedback loop |
| OPRO | Meta-prompt with trajectory | Yes | Yes (prompts) | Ascending sort, trajectory memory |
| SPO | Pairwise LLM output comparison | No | Yes (hill-climbing) | Reference-free OvO evaluation, 3 samples |
| BPO | Seq2seq rewriter (LLaMA-2-7B) | Preference data | No (amortized) | Per-prompt rewriting, model-agnostic |
| InstructZero | Bayesian optimization | Yes | Yes | Continuous proxy space |

Each represents a progressively richer optimization signal. APE is random search with intelligent initialization. OPRO is hill-climbing with memory. SPO replaces ground-truth scoring with pairwise output comparison. BPO amortizes the entire search into a learned rewriting function. InstructZero is Bayesian surrogate optimization. The common limitation of APE, OPRO, and InstructZero: they receive only scalar feedback (a score). They know *how well* a prompt performed, but not *why* it succeeded or failed, and not *which direction* to move. SPO replaces scalars with pairwise preferences, and BPO replaces search with a trained model, but neither provides directional feedback about *what to change*. That directional information is what the next section provides.

::: {.exercise-fillin}

Complete the missing description in this progression of generate-and-select methods:

1. APE: One-shot generation with **no memory** of past evaluations
2. {B|A: Population-based search with crossover and mutation operators|B: Iterative refinement with a trajectory of (prompt, score) pairs stored in a meta-prompt|C: Textual gradient critiques that describe why specific failures occurred}
3. InstructZero: Bayesian optimization with a full **probabilistic surrogate model** over the search space

::: {.fillin-feedback}
**Correct: B (OPRO).** The progression is in the richness of optimization memory. APE has no memory (one-shot). OPRO adds a trajectory of past (prompt, score) pairs in its meta-prompt, giving the optimizer in-context memory of what has been tried. InstructZero builds the richest model: a Gaussian process that captures the entire objective landscape. Option A describes evolutionary methods (EvoPrompt, covered in @sec-evolutionary), not the generate-and-select progression. Option C describes textual gradient methods (ProTeGi/TextGrad, covered in @sec-textual-gradients).
:::
